notes:
I've put together notes for all 18 verses. Coverage is uneven. I had to work from search-result excerpts of some pages, especially the full Pulpit Commentary and Enduring Word pages. Ellicott and Gill are thin: I could only fetch Ellicott's notes on v. 13, and Gill only shows up through his note on v. 1 and a reference to him in another commentary on v. 13.

**General point:** Most of the disagreement isn't between denominations. On v. 2, writers within the same tradition give different answers.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading.** Gill calls the book "the preacher's sermon," one connected discourse. He cites the Targum (the Aramaic paraphrase), which calls it Solomon's prophecy. Gill: "Or the preacher's sermon. The whole book is one continued discourse… The Targum is, 'the words of the prophecy, which the preacher, who is Solomon, prophesied.'" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/1-1.htm
- **The word "Qoheleth."** The Pulpit Commentary says it is a feminine noun from a verb meaning "to call," better translated "Convener" or "Debater," and found only in this book.  https://biblehub.com/ecclesiastes/1-1.htm
- **Guzik:** the title means someone who gathers, leads or speaks to a congregation.  https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Ecc/Ecc_1.cfm
- **Precept Austin (Bruce Hurt)** argues the author must be Solomon, since he was the only son of David to reign as king over Israel. He leans towards Solomon writing it in old age. It also quotes Stevenson, who notes that all three titles (Preacher, Son of David, king in Jerusalem) can apply to Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-1-commentary
- **Where the traditions differ: who wrote it, and was it a confession?**
  - *Ellicott (Anglican):* if "son of David" is taken strictly, it must mean Solomon. Taken loosely, it could be a later Davidic king such as Manasseh.  In the end he finds the internal arguments against Solomon decisive unless outside evidence turns up.  He also says there is "no warrant" for the popular view that the book is Solomon's repentance in old age.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/1.htm
  - *Pulpit Commentary:* it notes that, unlike Proverbs and Song of Songs, the title doesn't actually name Solomon.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/1-1.htm
  - *Charles Bridges (Anglican evangelical)* holds the opposite view: the words point to Solomon "with absolute precision," and the book is "mainly a book of confession."  https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62049/
  - *James MacDonald (quoted on Precept Austin)* says Qoheleth combines "the Penitent and the Preacher." https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-1-commentary
  - *Kaiser (quoted on Precept Austin)* notes that the evangelical scholars Delitzsch and Kidner doubted Solomon wrote it. He argues the language argument for a late date has been weakened since Fredericks's 1988 study. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-1-commentary
- **Catholic/Orthodox.** Gregory the Wonderworker's paraphrase presents Solomon, "king and prophet," addressing the whole Church of God.  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0602.htm

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading (Guzik).** This is the Preacher's first conclusion, not his last. "Vanity of vanities" is a Hebrew way of saying "the ultimate," like "holy of holies."  Guzik calls the book's claims "true lies": they are true if God doesn't matter, but that starting point is wrong.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-1/
- **Precept Austin:** the verse means everything is temporary and unsatisfying apart from God. It is not meant to promote scepticism.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-1-commentary
- **Where readers differ: "meaningless" or "fleeting"?**
  - *Meaningless apart from God.* GotQuestions (evangelical) supports "meaningless" and says life apart from God is empty.  https://www.gotquestions.org/all-is-vanity.html
  - *Fleeting, not pointless.* Ligonier (Reformed) says the phrase is not a claim that life is meaningless. Hebel means "vapour" or "breath": something fleeting and hard to grasp.  https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/vanity-vanities
  - Desiring God (Baptist) follows Iain Provan in rejecting "existential meaninglessness." It stresses life's brevity.  https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/is-all-really-vanity
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey).** The traditional "vanity" comes from Jerome's Latin Vulgate (4th century). Modern versions use "futile," "pointless," "meaningless" or "smoke."  Michael Fox (1988) proposed "absurd," borrowing from Camus, for cases where expectations don't match reality.  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/vanity-of-vanities/
- **Catholic.** Augustine says the things themselves aren't vain, since God made them. Rather, people subject themselves by sin to things that should serve them.  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1401.htm Chrysostom quotes the verse to defend counting earthly things as "a shadow, and a dream."  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220111.htm

**v. 3**
- **"Profit"** is a business word: life "pays no dividends." Guzik links it to Mark 8:36. "Under the sun" (used over 25 times in the book) means life in the material world, seen without eternity.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-1/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the word for "profit" (yithron) is found only in this book. The book's ending (12:13) answers the question.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm
- **Eaton (quoted on Precept Austin):** if a person's resources are only this-worldly, "No profit" is written over everything he does.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-1-commentary
- **Catholic.** Augustine reads vv. 2–3 as the text for a list of "the calamities and delusions of this life."  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120120.htm

**v. 4**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the Hebrew is literally "a generation goes, a generation comes." Man is only a pilgrim on earth.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm
- **Guzik:** this opens a series of nature examples showing that little seems to change.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-1/
- **Gregory of Nyssa:** the earth outlasts every generation, yet passing humans in their vanity think they are its lords.  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2907.htm

**vv. 5–7**
- **The Pulpit Commentary takes one image per verse:** v. 4 earth, v. 5 sun, v. 6 wind, v. 7 waters.  On the wind, it says even the freest thing in creation is bound to endless repetition.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm
- **Ancient versions on v. 6.** The Greek, Latin and Syriac versions apply v. 6 to the sun. The Pulpit Commentary prefers to read it as the wind only.  Ellicott agrees: reading it as the sun is "probably erroneous."  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ecclesiastes-1.html
- **Guzik and Eaton:** in the Old Testament, creation praises the Lord. Take God away, and creation shows only human weariness.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-1/
- **Applying v. 7 (F. B. Meyer, quoted by Guzik):** all the rivers of earthly joy will never fill the heart, but Christ makes all things new.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Ecc/Ecc_1.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** a "cosmic treadmill" of constant motion with no lasting change.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-1-commentary
- **MacLaren (Baptist)** reads v. 7 as the water cycle: rivers, rising vapour, rain, rivers again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/1-13.htm

**v. 8**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament) takes the Hebrew word dabar as "word": "All words are wearisome." It also cites Motais: man is bound by the same law as the world around him.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm
- **Guzik (quoting Adam Clarke):** for all his work, seeing and hearing, man remains unsatisfied. Endless desire for gain and endless curiosity keep him going.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-1/

**v. 9**
- **Guzik:** new things soon grow old. But believers born of the Spirit don't live "under the sun" in this sense; their lives are full of new things.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-1/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the Greek and Latin versions phrase the verse as questions. What was said about nature is now said about human life, both actions and morals.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm

**v. 10**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** seeming new things are earlier discoveries that were forgotten and then revived.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm

**v. 11**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** read "former men," not "former things." It quotes Marcus Aurelius on how fame fades.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm
- **Guzik:** the futility stretches into both past and future; all is forgotten.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-1/

**v. 12**
- **Guzik:** Solomon was famous for his wisdom, a gift from God (1 Kings 3–4). If wisdom could find the answer, he was the man to find it.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-1/
- **Precept Austin** says this verse leaves no doubt Solomon is the author.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-1-commentary
- **Pulpit Commentary:** it reads the speaker as Solomon brought back as a literary figure ("Solomon redivivus"). It notes that "king over Israel" points to a time before the kingdom split.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm

**v. 13** (the verse where commentators most clearly disagree)
- **Ellicott:** for the Hebrews, the "heart" is the seat of the mind, so "I gave my heart" means "I applied my mind." The margin's "to afflict them" is too strong a translation; better "to travail therein." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/1-13.htm
- **Benson (Methodist):** the hard task of searching is God's just punishment on mankind for eating from the tree of knowledge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/1-13.htm
- **A commentary on the same page, citing Gill:** man gets his knowledge, like his bread, by the sweat of his brow (Genesis 3:19). Another note takes it as God's chastening of curiosity.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/1-13.htm
- **Another note on that page (it reads like the Cambridge Bible):** God is first named in the book alongside the thought that this fruitless search is His appointment. He gives the desire, but not the full truth that satisfies it.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/1-13.htm
- **MacLaren (Baptist)** calls this verse a "gloomy half-truth." Hebrews 12:10 completes it: hardship is the Father's discipline, so that we share His holiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/1-13.htm
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel, on one of your Pentecostal/charismatic sites):** the sense of futility comes from God and shows His love. He made a God-shaped space in us (Augustine) and subjected creation to futility in hope (Romans 8:20).  https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Ecc/Ecc_1.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** God is called "Elohim" (the general word for God) throughout the book, never "Jehovah" (the covenant name). It says the theme is mankind's relation to God's providence, not Israel's own concerns.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm

**v. 14**
- **GotQuestions:** hebel here means not just "meaningless" but beyond understanding.  https://www.gotquestions.org/hevel-in-the-Bible.html
- **Bible Odyssey:** six times in the book, hevel is followed by "a chasing after wind," which adds to its meaning.  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/vanity-of-vanities/
- **Henry Morris (quoted on Precept Austin):** work done only "under the sun" vexes the spirit rather than satisfying it.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-1-commentary

**v. 15**
- **Kidner (quoted by Guzik):** all human thinking has twists ("crooked") and gaps ("lacking") that it cannot straighten out or fill.  https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Ecc/Ecc_1.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** nothing man can do fixes these flaws.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm

**v. 16**
- **Who were the kings "before me"?** Kidner (quoted by Guzik) says the claim rules out any successor to Solomon.  https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Ecc/Ecc_1.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary disagrees. It sees a slip by a later writer, implying a line of kings that the historical Solomon didn't have.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm
- Leon Hyatt (Precept Austin) answers that David was the only Israelite king in Jerusalem before Solomon.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62180/
- **Guzik:** "communed with my heart" shows a man looking inward for answers instead of to God.  https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Ecc/Ecc_1.cfm
- **Dionysius of Alexandria:** this was worldly wisdom that "puffs up," not the wisdom God gives.  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0613.htm

**v. 17**
- **Pulpit Commentary, citing Jerome:** he studied folly so as to understand wisdom by its opposite.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm
- **Guzik:** thinking harder was not the answer; it was all grasping at wind.  https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Ecc/Ecc_1.cfm

**v. 18**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the deeper the insight into human life, the more grief at its unfinished state. The sorrow is in oneself.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/1.htm
- **Eaton (quoted by Guzik):** wisdom limited to "under the sun" sees only restless repetition.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Ecc/Ecc_1.cfm
- **Matthew Henry:** the more he knew, the more cause he had to mourn. Learn to hate sin and rest in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/1-13.htm

---

**What I couldn't find:**
- Anything from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org).
- A Wesley's Notes page (wesley.nnu.edu) or a Pentecostal source other than Guzik.
- NET Bible notes or anything Orthodox from oca.org.
- Any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. None of the pages I read discuss it.
